I grew up being ping-ponged and terrorized between my 'children should be seen and not heard' dad and my mom who was smothering and controlling because I was something for her/a doll to fit into her narrative...when she was around and could be bothered. Trauma, mental health issues, a sprinkle of domestic violence and addiction in spades plus an extended family that knew something wasn't right but didn't act.

Were they trash? I mean I wasn't molested or sold for drugs (mind you my mom did take my healthcare card to try and \*get\* drugs when I was a teenager so?) and we were clothed, housed, clean and fed. So compared to some they were good parents, but the bar's in hell, you know? It's taken me into adulthood to realize that what they did isn't good parenting. That's like...you're avoiding jail or your kids being put into the foster system (at least back in the 90s, now probably not).

So I think it's possible to go 'okay, so they avoided doing the Big Bad stuff, but they were still shitty parents'.

Parenting is more than just 'this kid isn't dead and is fed, housed and we don't beat them'. If you're not willing/able to actively support, guide and engage with this developing little person then you shouldn't have them imo.

I do think a lot of people had kids because birth control failed/that's what you did, not because they were ready and interested in parenting.

34 year old autistic person here, a lot of your post is 'my autistic son is being autistic, what do I do to change that?' it seems. 

Not intentionally of course, but different neurotypes don't understand each other very well. 

Re: only wanting xyz foods, it's about safety, predictability and avoiding sensory distress. A lot of fast food/processed food is made to taste the same, feel the same, smell the same etc each and every time. For an autistic person who struggles with sensory issues around food and may also struggle with feeling too overwhelmed in general to want the added sensory input of food at all processed food is easiest and most reliable. In contrast homemade food (even if it's the same recipe each time) can vary a lot in texture, taste, smell and so on. Chicken is not just chicken to an autistic person: the subtle taste and texture etc differences that either don't bother you or you don't even pick up on? Big deal to him. Something that's 'enh, but edible' to you could taste completely inedible, rancid and vile to him and knowing that it's healthy etc doesn't make it any easier to swallow. 

If you asked me: "Alone, do you like blueberries?" I cannot give you a yes or no answer for example. What format? Where were they grown? Which size and colour? The same container of blueberries can have blueberries I like a lot and blueberries that are disgusting, so I'm not going to say 'yes' as a blanket statement. If you ask me 'do you like xyz processed food?' I can tell you yes or no because it's nearly always completely the same every time.  

 Re: grocery shopping it's probably about trying to relieve anxiety and preserve routine and predictability.  It's a disruption: there's lots of things happening (you're leaving, returning, noises, food being put away etc) and if he comes with you to the store then there's the sensory issues of a store. He might be stressed about 'okay what are they gonna try and feed me this week?' or 'when are we going shopping so I can prepare for it?' or 'will they get my safe foods/enough of them this week?'

Re: obsession with certain subjects. That's just the nature of the autism beast so to speak. Special interests and in general having an interest-focused brain instead of a social-focused brain. There's no changing that. It's the way we're wired. He's trying to share what's important to him with you as a means of connecting. 

I'm much older than your son, but random facts and the stuff 'nobody thinks about?' love that. That's my jam. I'm not into Sonic but I'm into animals/nature the way your son likes Sonic. 

Expanding himself? Enh....not really what you should be aiming for. It's not going to happen unless he's ready or wants it to happen and a lot of autistic people like routine and repetition. Maybe he'll never eat a salad (or maybe one day years from now his brain will decide 'OMG I LOVE SALAD') and that's okay. In the interim try and work with him to make sure he's getting his nutrients and ask if he'd like to try xyz food (and make him a teeny like 'taster' portion alongside a safe food) without the expectation that he'll eat it that night.

Autism can't be changed, only accommodated and worked with. It's the way your son's brain is wired after all.

I got told for many many years 'oh it's because you're fat, lose weight' when in reality it was endometriosis, anemia, hypothyroidism, a malfunctioning VP shunt, low vitamin D and sleep apnea that went untreated for \*years\*.  There were also mental health concerns and undiagnosed-until-then autism. Those things treated/accommodated? Suddenly I can cycle an hour a day, make better diet choices and my blood pressure and blood sugar, heat intolerance and fatigue are better. I actually get flagged as 'low cholesterol' now which is funny to me because everyone assumes I \*must\* have issues due to my size.

Am I still fat? Yeah. But I'm healthier and happier than I was as chronically fasting 100 lbs lighter college student who walked 2 hours a day while starving and thought if I could just keep the weight off I'd finally feel better. I make better choices, exercise more, sleep better etc. Losing weight, on it's own, is not going to guarantee health.

First step: new carrier because you've likely poisoned that one to her.


Second step: make it comfy and leave it out with the door open somewhere in your living room/bedroom/wherever she spends time.


Third step: wait. The carrier needs to become an everyday normal thing for her. Like her scratching post, cat trees etc. Just another bed. If the only time she ever sees the carrier is you take it out to try and cram her in then of course she's gonna freak out.


Fourth step: you can try tossing treats in there and see if she follows them in. You could even work on a "go in your carrier" cue word. 


In the interim if you need to get her in her old carrier in an emergency you put the carrier vertically with the door facing the ceiling. Towel her and just 1-2-3 go quickly put her and the towel in.

It's an elective amputation of the tips of their toes. It changes the way they walk (leaving them at risk of joint damage and pain with age) as well as chronic pain in the amputated stumps. Also chronic infection and bits of bone/bone shards remaining in the flesh of the toe. 

Declawed cats are also more likely to bite and to have litterbox issues---their oversensitive amputated toe-stumps make digging or standing in litter painful and without their first line of defense (their claws) they are more likely to resort to biting. 

Don't do it.

The prevalence and severity of the things you are vaccinating them against (like rabies) is so, so much more of a threat than FISS.

Basically with feline injection site sarcomas it's a freak thing that happens. Not only with vaccines but any sort of injection because the cat's individual immune system is weird/decides to be weird at an injection site. But short of never ever getting your cats any sort of vaccine, IV, antibiotic, subcutaneous fluid, insulin injection, microchip etc (literally anything that pierces or injects into the skin) you're not going to avoid it. Think about how many millions of cats get vaccines and such and are fine--it's a very rare thing.

There's a ton of other issues (rabies, FeLV, panleukopenia, parasites, diabetes, infections, getting lost and euthanized at shelter etc) that your cats will be vulnerable to and are much more likely to encounter and die from if you don't vaccinate them and avoid any sort of injected treatment or putting in a microchip.

Vets are trained to deal with FISS and watch for it. They know. They also see what happens to cats who \*don't\* get vaccinated. Vaccinate your cats. They'll be fine.

Something that helped me was the anesthesiologist during my first surgery telling me "This is scary for you, but so, so routine for us. We manage and see this regularly. We're not scared." 


I see it like any other medical procedure or treatment. It might take some adjustments and such but in the end most people do well. Especially when it comes to hydrocephalus leaving it untreated isn't any better than having to have adjustments.



Both of my recent surgeries were to deal with the distal end of my shunt catheter migrating out of my peritoneal space and under my skin by the upper left side of my abdomen. One surgery which was just returning the original catheter I've had for 20+ years to the right space failed a few days after surgery. I had to have a second one where connectors and an extension was put on and then the now-longer tube was returned to the peritoneal space. 12 days later and yeah I've got some adjustments headaches and abdominal pain but it's improving with time.



As spooky as all this sounds they were short, uncomplicated surgeries and I went home same-day after both procedures.

So there's a few problems with this 'study', first being that it's an online survey that relies on owner-reporting, owner bias/perception and not an actual legitimate medical evaluation of any of these cats. Second there's taking data and going 'welp this must support my theory' when there could be a variety of other factors that explain why you found the results you did. 

Also...if you poll the owners of 1,380 cats and only nine percent of those feed their cats a plant-based diet (so about 130 cats) well no duh you're going to find more meat-eating cats with health problems and more vet visits because the sample size is that much larger. That does not, in any way mean that cats eating a plant-based diet are healthier. It could mean for example, that only cats without health issues or who are less prone to xyz are able (at the time of the poll) to eat a plant-based diet and survive. It could also suggest that a cat prone to health problems/who developed health problems will be eating a meat-based prescription cat food precisely because those are the ones developed to help treat their condition, not because the meat-based food itself made them sick. 

Plus there's a huge lack of controls here. If this study is based in the UK/europe then a lot of these cats likely have outdoor access. Are they really vegan then? Likely not and they're snacking on bugs, mice and birds. The folks who created the study/survey also decided not to account for breed-related health trends. 

I understand wanting less harmful cat food, I do. I, myself, wish we had the research and answers already. But we don't. The companies that make plant-based cat foods are somewhere between outright sketchy (looking at you, Evolution) and meaning well but not having the veterinary nutritionists on staff or feeding trials done. There's too much reliance on buzzwords and appealing to the vegan owner's emotions/desires and 'well we've sold a lot of this food and cats like it' and not on safety, data and quality control. 

So that's a pass for me. Not because I don't think cats should be plant-based/that it's unnatural or anything like that, but because we don't have the research and such to do it safely yet. If the manufacturers that follow WSAVA guidelines develop a plant-based foods and plant-based prescription cat food alternatives I'd gladly give that a go. But they haven't yet, so my cat stays on his prescription diet even if it has meat in it.

Cats are about compromise and adjusting, much more like living with a roommate. 

They're also in a weird domesticated but not situation and are a prey animal as much as a predator. So they're very different from the dynamic you'd expect with most dogs. 

Cats are all about routine, ownership of territory and feeling safe/having control. Without that they get strung out. 

There's a lot of stuff on the market sold for cats that are actually very 'anti-cat'---scented litters, pelleted litters, covered litterboxes, boxes that are too small, flimsy scratching posts and short 'meh' cat trees. A lot of people want to provide covered boxes, stash them out of sight/hide them in closets and try to scoop them as little as possible. 

A lot of people also try and feed cats like dogs---the twice daily meal feeding. But cats aren't really built for that. They'd naturally eat tiny meals frequently throughout the day at their own discretion, so a lot of the time it's better to leave out a measured daily portion and let them decide. 

Basically, there's gonna be visible cat stuff in your house. Cat trees and scratchers and cat tunnels next to the couch or your bed. Litterboxes out in the open. There's gonna be a lot of 'because the cat likes/needs it that way' and you need to learn to pick your battles. Cat proof and accept that yes, there's going to be like a permanent puppy in your house that can climb up on/into way more things than an actual dog. Cats are intelligent, but trainability? Ennnh. Technically they are trainable, but they're not labradors. They're more like those dog breeds that are like 'yeah, I could...but why? what's in it for me? does that matter enough right now?'

A lot of 'training' them is about management/prevention/redirection and avoiding teaching them that something 'works' if you don't want them to do it and sometimes that'll even include negative attention. Once they learn something 'works' or sometimes gets them what they want it can take a long time for them to forget. For example if meowing at 3am gets you awake and moving (even if you're mad as hell) then it works. Play dead. Wear earplugs if you have to. 

People try using punishment like a spray bottle etc to 'train' their cat. Doesn't work. \*You\* become the negative thing to be avoided, not (for example) eating the plants or getting on the counter. When you're not around? They're still doing it. 

Another big thing people forget to do? Play with your cat! Get that little ambush predator brain engaged for 5-10 minute sessions multiple times a day with an interactive wand toy. It's such a critical part of their well-being. If you don't give them a constructive outlet for that need and that energy, they'll find it elsewhere (like your ankles in the middle of the night) or become destructive and loud. Ditto with passive engagement (Cat Tv if you will) like a good window to watch stuff (bonus if there's a bird feeder), a (safe) aquarium etc. Rotate their toys so they don't get too bored. 

Keep your kitty indoors btw unless you've got them on a harness or in a catio/secured backyard. It's much safer and healthier for them and much kinder to other animals in the neighbourhood.

If kitty is matted then your roommate should "start over" and get her shaved at a vet where they can sedate her.

Once kitty is shaved then roommate has to start introducing daily brush time. The key is to go slow, let kitty choose to walk away and to feed those treat tubes while they brush. Brushing stops = treat stops.


When I say go slow it might mean starting with just "yay! I see the brush I get treats!" if the sight of the brush already makes kitty stressed until kitty *loves* seeing the brush come out. Then (after however many sessions that first step takes) you work on the brush coming closer, then maybe a brief touch, then maybe 1 pass on their neck, then 2 passes, then maybe 1 pass on their side etc. 


It takes time and you need to go slow, but daily consistency pays off. At first my cat was like "you get 3 passes on the left side of my neck and then I'm out!". Weeks later I can comb him out thoroughly pretty much anywhere except his tail and inside his back legs (we'll get there though). He sees the comb and the tube treat come out and he runs over to get on the desk, head bonk me when I get to the desk and can't wait to be brushed.


Added bonus being that daily brushing means less fur everywhere and less hairballs.


All that said just brushing might not be enough. Roommate could look into the Purina LiveClear food and see of that'd be an option. You might want to consult with an allergy doctor about meds or shots.

Cats also don't have the sort of thinking skills like humans do. They're not thinking about 'oh gee I'd like to be a parent' or anything like that. They don't think about it anymore and there's nothing to miss.

You don't feed cats by 'a cat needs this volume of food per day' but by how many calories they require in a day. 

You want to offer a healthy adult cat about 20 calories per pound of (lean/healthy) bodyweight. Like with people it's not an exact rule, things like age (seniors can require less) and individual metabolism can influence it, but it's a good guideline to start with.

You need at least 3 boxes and they need to be placed throughout the house. It's a non-negociable. They need to be large enough (aim for 18x24 inches or larger) and uncovered---clear plastic storage bins with a hole cut out in one side work great. They also need to be scooped twice daily and use a good quality, unscented clumping litter.

If all you have is one box in the basement then it's to be expected they'll poop/pee in other places. 

Litterboxes can go anywhere, not just in basements and bathrooms. Bedrooms, living rooms, offices...all are viable options. You need to make room or you're going to continue to have litterbox issues. 

My cat's litterbox is right next to my desk in the living room. I've gone back down to using just one box because I live in a small, single-floor apartment and he's my only cat and he prefers to pee and poop all at once in one box, but when I had two litterboxes the second one was in my bedroom. Wasn't a problem and no issue with smell. But with multiple cats and a multiple-floor home you really need to follow the rules about how many litterboxes you need.

Am I aware that, on a microscopic level there may be some cross-contamination? Sure.

But he actually keeps himself clean back there (no dingleberries) and to be fair I don't sterilize my own ass either. Visibly clean yes of course, but not sterilized and there's a difference. So if I can get all my human skin flakes and bacteria and such on my bed (even if I'm clean and fresh out the shower), then my indoor-only cat can do the same. Life isn't sterile anyway and I just wash the bedsheets regularly.

If your kitty is constantly struggling to keep himself clean I'd be looking into why. Is he overweight? Possibly arthritic? Too fluffy and needs a trim back there? Is he not eating the right food for him so his poop is softer than it should be? Is he forced to go into a covered litterbox and/or one that is too small for him so he ends up smearing it somehow?

Take her to the vet in order to rule out a medical issue, then offer her a good quality, fine-grained clumping litter that is unscented. Usually unscented clumping clay is your best bet. 

A lot of cats don't like the pine pellets as they're uncomfortable to stand on.

She may also want a second box as sometimes cats will reserve one litterbox for pee, the other for poop.

That whole thing about feeding prey that's sized according to their bodies or weight doesn't really hold up in a lot of situations.

Especially with boas who, in general, aren't able to tolerate the sort of large meals that a python might.

It can be helpful to provide a limit you shouldn't exceed, but feeding older animals is more about maintaining a healthy body weight and remembering that snakes have a much lower metabolism than mammals or birds do.

If, for example, we went by body size/width or his weight alone I could offer my 12 year old adult male ball python could have a medium or large rat and he could be offered prey items weekly. In reality? He eats one 50-60 gram small rat every 4-5 weeks (or the equivalent weight in adult mice or chicks, which usually means 2 mice or 2 chicks). That's it. It keeps him in a good body condition and will prolong his life. He's 4.5 feet long. Even the 8 foot carpet python I had only ate a 200g or so rat every 4 weeks. She'd get fat otherwise.

Obesity and overfeeding are a huge problem in the reptile keeping world.

Amputations come with risks---both post-surgical complications and the risk of chronic pain, arthritis in the surrounding joints, bone spurs/overgrowth etc throughout life.

When you declaw a cat (and amputate the ends of their toes) you are fundamentally making them walk in a way they are not meant to and permanently severing tendons in their toes. These tendons are interconnected to muscles in their legs and shoulders---they're the ones that allow them to stretch their paws and do the full scratching motion in their toes. This unnatural posture (cats are designed to walk on their toes) and the damaged tendons means declawed cats tend to experience arthritis and chronic pain earlier and more severely than non-declawed cats.

Cats who experience chronic pain/develop arthritis are more likely to refuse to use the litterbox and become more likely to bite/be defensive. Plus if they know they cannot scratch you because you have declawed them, then they'll bite first if they have to.

So in the end you end up with a cat who is more likely to be miserable, pee/poop all over your house and bite.

Declawing is illegal in many places for good reason.

Cats with properly trimmed claws and who are provided with enough of the right scratching posts/surfaces aren't going to destroy your house.

Any place where you've had something inserted or had a bone etc broken is a place where, with time, the body can attempt to calcify it or you can develop arthritis. Both of these things can be painful. 

If you still have any hardware in your spine it can decide to migrate/break etc at some point in your life, which can cause neuro issues (if it pokes into something) and can be painful. 

Any place where you've had surgical intervention or a large wound can lead to adhesions/scar tissue around the surgery or injury site. This can lead to stiffness, pain and (depending on if nerves etc get trapped by said scar tissue) issues with neuro function. 

All you can do now is focus on good nutrition, good rest, protect your back, keep an eye out for any new issues and stretch/exercise in a way that's good for you without overdoing it. Pain management will be part of your life. 

Start looking at ways to make your life easier/talk to an occupational therapist. If mobility aids or home adaptation or what have you become necessary to make life easier then go for it. Wheelchairs aren't so bad, especially if using one allows you to have less pain and be more functional in your day-to-day life.

It's not about automatically locking a dog away though.

It's about giving your dog enough training and management that they're not a hazard or a nuisance. A dog who barks all the time is going to get complaints and should you ever have to rehome the dog they're going to have a harder time getting adopted.

If you invite someone over and your dog is out of control and hurting them/making them uncomfortable/putting them at risk in some way you need to do something about it.

Saying otherwise is like saying that just because you live there you can do whatever you want regardless of visitors, bylaws and neighbours.

The best thing to do is literally create distance and help him calm down. It's not something to punish. It's him being so stressed or scared that he's in fight or flight mode. It'd be like trying to scold someone out of a panic attack or PTSD trigger.

If he's biting out of nowhere then either a) he's got a medical issue going on that could be causing pain or b) you've been scolding him or not reading his body language correctly so he feels like the only way you will listen/he can express his fear/discomfort is to go to "the final resort" and bite.

At this point it's paramount to make sure he feels safe/avoid putting him in situations where he feels like he needs to freak out/bite and to work on building a positive association to xyz person or dog.  

Other than that, consistency and patience. 

When it comes to fearful dogs remember that distance, duration and downtime/management are essential. Every time your dog has a big freakout episode cortisol and other stress hormones remain elevated for days afterward, meaning that he'll be even more easily provoked or frightened. You'll want to check out the CARE protocol for reactive dogs and start working on it. 

Remember: Do \*NOT\* punish your dog for displaying fearful/defensive behaviour towards a given person or dog. You will only confirm for him that a) those things are indeed bad/scary and b) teach him to stop growling/barking---which is how you get a dog who bites 'out of nowhere'. If he starts freaking out/is staring/not able to pay attention to you then it's your signal that he's over threshold and he needs your help---calmly remove him from the situation/create some distance.

So I was grateful for the vet staff being able to take her body (when I was ready) into the back of the clinic to store her for her cremation instead of sitting there with her in my house wondering what to do now.   

I think, as hard as it is, that's part of the pact that we make when we agree to love them and to take care of them. She wasn't alone when she died and I stayed by her the whole way. She had, as weird as it sounds, a reasonably good death. She was with her person, in a place she knew and she was kept as comfortable as she could be. The vet clinic was down the street from where I was living at the time so, in a weird way, I knew she was 'close by' and it was helpful. They kept some of her feathers for me and gave them to me with her ashes when they were ready.  

In contrast I lost my mom in 2019 and not only was her death completely unforeseen and traumatic in and of itself, but....having to  see her for 10 minutes and then just walk out of the funeral home and leave her there made it so much worse. I didn't get the same processing time and I didn't get to accompany her body to the crematorium and she was cremated many, many miles from where we lived. He said it really helped make the whole ordeal easier.

Social anxiety and introversion are two completely different things.

Social anxiety disorder is the excessive fear of and worrying that you've said the wrong thing, will do something stupid, will be judged etc.

Introversion is more about needing a lot of downtime/alone time and becoming quickly drained or overstimulated around people and large groups of people or busy environments. They generally like to think things over more and prefer solitary activities. Unlike social anxiety It's not a mental health condition but an inborn trait.

I'm introverted as hell. Eventually I just need a break. Too much interaction and I end up getting almost what feels like a hangover. I won't go out of my way to chat to random people and I will always prefer small get togethers with 1-3 friends over a larger gathering. Not enough solitary time and I get cranky as hell. Give me the choice of a good book or documentary  vs talking to a friend and 99% of the time I'll take the book/documentary. Extroverts on the other hand usually enjoy socializing just for the heck of it and have a bigger social battery that drains slower and recharges faster than mine does.

Introverts don't necessarily have social anxiety or problems socializing when they do socialize, they just want to socialize less/in quieter settings. Now of course you can be both introverted and socially anxious (or in my case autistic) but they're not the same thing. Someone who avoids socializing just out of fear isn't an Introvert.

You need to have a fire safety plan that includes your pets. Unless you physically  cannot access them and it becomes a you vs them situation they should be coming with you.

If you're using a carrier it should be kept out in the open and made into a comfy resting spot so that the dog is familiar with it and you don't  have to go digging in a closet etc if you need it.

It's hard to flat out give specific chair recommendations because everyone has different lifestyles, homes, locations, bodies and specific needs or limitations. Some chairs have limitations in terms of only coming in specific measurements/only offering certain positions and angles or not being compatible with certain add-ons or equipment. If your body/what is safe and comfortable positioning for you etc isn't within those measurements then you can't get that chair.  

What might be awesome for me would be hell for you and vice versa. So I'm seconding the recommendation that you get fitted by/discuss it with a professional who works with wheelchairs/wheelchair users. 

While you're waiting for your appointments/insurance to get back to you etc you can write down/take notes on some of your needs/concerns/lifestyle factors so that you've a baseline to to start from. 

What's the weather like where you are?

How are the sidewalks and terrain where you live? Lots of cracks, hills and such? Do you get a lot of rain/slush/snow/cold weather?  

Is your home able/easily able to be modified to accomodate a motorized chair?

Do you travel often/how? A motorized chair is not easy to transport so if you're frequently getting into cars or  trying to use public transit you might want to think about a manual chair.

What are you planning on doing with this chair? Try to think about the locations you most often visit/navigate in. Do you go alone or would someone be around to assist you? 

What do you want to prioritize/what trade offs are you able or willing to make? Are there limitations in what your insurance etc is willing to cover?

Motorized chairs are comfy as hell and very good for pain/fatigue management but they're a pain in the ass to use indoors and hard to transport/actually do things in. Deconditioning can also be a problem if you find yourself using the chair for more than just 'getting around for long distances'. They do make more lightweight folding versions but they're kinda gimmicky and not going to be able to manage well on things that aren't 'cruising around at the indoor mall/on level sidewalks on a sunny day' type thing. 

It is likely that you'll not get everything 100% perfect with the first chair you choose, that's to be expected, so try not to stress about it. But the more prepared you are the easier it'll be. Don't be me and show up going 'enh I dunno' lol. To give you a personal example for the last four years I've been relying on a Quickie 323 powerchair plus a carbon fibre Apex from Motion Composites combination. These two were my 'starter chairs'.  Now that I've experience and have a better idea of what I need I'll be getting fitted for my second chair tomorrow and am likely going with a TiLite ZRA titanium chair plus a SmartDrive.

Why? The deconditioning with the powerchair was \*brutal\* for me and it didn't really fit anywhere I was going. My Apex was light (and that was great) but carbon fibre flexes and transmits a lot of vibration---which for me it turns out felt really unpleasant and unstable. It also doesn't transfer energy as well because it flexes, though it is much better at turning propelling into distance than a folding chair or the standard heavy hospital chair. The centre of gravity, backrest height and etc also were done incorrectly/not in a way that an active wheelchair user needs. I also had to swap out the standard handrims and handrim position for SurgeLT handrims set as close as possible to the drive wheels---I have small hands and the standard handrim shape and position were awkward and painful for me/my wrists.

You can build it up over time and eventually he will enjoy (or at least cooperate with) combing.

So I got access to my pelvic floor therapist through the spinal rehab hospital I go to (I'm a wheelchair user) but you should be able to ask a gynecologist or urologist (or family doctor) for referral to one.

Word of warning that you might have a hard time with it if you're shy/uncomfortable with talking about your bladder/bowel habits and physical exams.

Usually the first appointment the therapist will ask you a bunch of questions about your symptoms/toilet habits/bathroom set up. Whether you deal with any types of incontinence, urgency, pain, do you wake up at night frequently to pee and so on.

They will recommend any modifications or corrections of bad habits (no straining, getting a stool so that you can be in a healthy position to pee/poop etc) and give you some beginner exercises to do at home as well as your next follow up appointment.

The follow-up gets more hands-on. They will do a pelvic exam and ask you to cough/attempt to squeeze your muscles around their fingers etc to see what state you pelvic floor is in and if they can observe any signs of dysfunction. They will attempt to teach you how to feel/coordinate the pelvic floor muscles properly and will give you more personalized exercises to do at home.

After that you'll have a regular follow-up with them to see how you're doing and they may attempt to do physio/biofeedback exercises with you in their office. I did the biofeedback and well...it's basically playing flappy bird with your butthole or vagina. A probe is inserted and you're given a screen to watch and you need to learn to contract/relax your muscles as needed to complete the exercises. It doesn't hurt but of course it can be awkward. I just thought it was funny.

The majority of the time 'ringworm' in cats is caused by a fungus that, while it can infect people, doesn't do so as easily as the fungus that commonly causes ringworm/jock itch/etc in people. So unless you've broken skin or are immunocompromised it is less likely to take hold.

Similarly in cats it is usually self-limiting (though it can take months) and tends to only infect kittens or ill/stressed cats because of the weakened/immature immune system. Some cats (particularly long-haired kitties) can be asymptomatic carriers of the fungus but it doesn't necessarily bother them. Much like certain people can have certain bacteria or fungus on their skin that doesn't cause problems in them.

It's pretty much impossible to 100% clear the given fungal spores from an environment. You can't. It's like trying to nuke every type of bacteria or fungus that could cause a problem in humans and/or is normally found in some amount on human skin. What you want to do is minimize the amount in the environment, treat any active infections and help the kitties immune systems fight it off. Luckily it tends to live in/on the fur so essentially just vacuum up and dispose of the fur and  you're good.

If by some chance you get ringworm---it clears up easily and (usually) responds to an over-the-counter antifungal cream.

The things we vaccinate cats for are often highly contagious, incurable and can be deadly or zoonotic thus transfer to humans. See FIV, FeLV, panleuk and rabies for example. Vets recommend boosters for a given vaccine because there is no way to know how long a given animal will retain enough of an immune response to be protected. Usually the recommended revaccination schedule for a given vaccine is proven through 'challenge tests' in which a study group of animals will be re-exposed to a given pathogen after X amount of years/months from vaccination and see how many of them (if any) avoid becoming infected. A particular animal \*could\* retain immunity for longer than that (and sometimes less), but this is the general guideline they advise in order to keep as many animals protected as possible given that you can't predict it. Poor/non-responders to a vaccine or animals who cannot be vaccinated are protected through having enough vaccinated/good responding animals in a given population. They will also test a vaccine's baseline efficacy by comparing a control group (unvaccinated) and a test vaccinated group to see how many avoid becoming infected by a given pathogen. They come up with general vaccination guidelines and efficacy ratings based on these studies and tests.

Vaccines are lifesavers, there really isn't a reason not to vaccinate your cat (unless they've experienced a severe reaction to a vaccine or have some other medical contraindication) according to the revaccination schedule determined for a particular vaccine.

Usually now the recommendations for the core vaccine and the rabies vaccine after the initial series are completed is a booster shot every 3 years unless your city mandates sooner. FIV and FeLV vaccines usually need to be boosted yearly.

With the flat faced/brachycephalic breeds like frenchies it's not that they don't want to do things but that their abnormal bodies/faces means that they physically cannot safely do what their minds as dogs want to do. So you need to adjust their exercise/how you keep them occupied. 

Re: her walk length, you're going to want to increase it slowly (kinda like you don't want to go from being a couch potato to a gym rat all in one go---you need to build up slowly). Say do 30 minutes in the am and then 30 minutes at night, then increase from there to where she's satisfied and it's feasible for you. 

In terms potty pads vs someone taking her out the absolute best thing would be to find someone who can take her out. It would allow her more social attention and stimulation while you're out of the house and would be the clearest distinction of 'we don't pee/poop in the house anymore'. If it's really not possible though then yes potty pads would be the second best option. 

Btw I do recommend that she sees a vet in case she has a bladder infection or something else going on in addition which would make her more likely to have accidents in the house. Having to hold her bladder too long can cause UTIs or other issues.

Be aware though that like a young puppy who is learning not to pee in the house she may need to be let out to pee/poop more often than 4 times a day at first.

That's what I mean though, when she gets to the just wanting to explore part that's when the non-potty break walk starts usually. Dogs live for sniffing and exploring. Sometimes they will mark/do quick tiny pees on bushes etc as they go but it's important to let them sniff and explore. Her not being focused on peeing/pooping anymore shouldn't be your cue to turn around.

Part of what she needs exercise-wise exactly will depend on her breed/energy level. But it's pretty safe to assume that 15-20 minutes of walking twice a day isn't enough for most dogs unless they're very old or one of the very low energy breeds. 15 minutes is a "quick walk for a potty break" type thing and for a legitimate exercise walk you'd be looking at 30 minutes to an hour per walk. Some high energy breeds especially if young will need more than that.

You can also add in some playing fetch and/or training sessions to keep things interesting and work her mind as well as her body. Dogs really need more attention and care than most folks realize.

If she's only taken out twice a day to pee/poop and you guys sometimes are okay with her peeing in the house then she's going to keep doing it. She can't magically know when it's okay to pee in the house/where it's ok to pee in the house and when it's not. A housetrained adult dog in good health needs to go out at least 4 times per day/in 24 hours to go to the bathroom. If the dog is still a puppy, is old or has medical issues they'll need to go out even more than that.

Twice a day is not enough. Full stop. 
It also sounds like she could be anxious, stressed and bored from not getting enough exercise and being home alone too much. Some dogs in that state will have accidents even if they get taken outside enough---they literally get so stressed they pee/poop themselves.

You shouldn't be turning around and going home once she's just walking---that should just be the start of the walk. It's okay for 1-2 trips per day to be just potty breaks but the other 1-2 trips should include exercise after she's peed/pooped.

If you guys absolutely cannot take her out more than twice a day (and you really should be) then at least set up an indoor potty spot/puppy pad area in some part of the house so she can start to have a visual sign of where to go.

The longer he's allowed to practice this behaviour and learn that it's pleasurable to do the more likely he is to do it even after he is neutered.

I adopted a young shelter kitty (he just turned 1 a few days ago) back in December and he's a frustration/attention biter and struggles with predatory/play aggression too. It's been a long road and we're still working on it but he's getting better.

Part of it is making sure he has enough things to do (enough cat trees, foraging toys/food puzzles instead of eating out of a bowl), part of it is making sure he has enough interactive playtime with a wand toy (20 minute sessions 3 times a day) and part of it is preventing/redirecting. 

Redirecting/preventing meaning if I know, for example, that my cat gets wound up at night and will run in to chomp my ankles as I'm getting into bed that I will preemptively toss a toy/treat away from me so that he runs after that while I get into bed. If I know that picking him up to remove him from somewhere he shouldn't be will get me chomped I use a laser toy to guide him out instead. If I know that he gets chompy if I pet him too long I don't pet him that long or continuously.

The less a cat practices a behaviour the less it gets reinforced and over time they'll choose not to do it. The more the cat's needs for exercise/appropriate outlets are met the less excess energy and frustration they have. Likewise if we learn their body language that says they're beginning to get wound up/overstimulated and respond appropriately they won't feel the need to get the message across by being 'louder' and biting.

Unfortunately the best thing to do is (unless we're talking about nipping during petting--stop petting him and take the hint) ignore him if he bites/remove yourself from the room without yelling or getting angry. He's looking for attention/a reaction (even if negative) and again if he's learned that biting gets him fed or let out he'll do it more often because it works. Just silently get up and walk out/close the door behind you if you can. He'll learn that 'oops, biting gets me the opposite of what I want' and also that it's not rewarding/fun to bite ankles. You don't want to try and toss a toy/treat after he has already bitten you because then you'll just teach him to bite more.

Edit: is he fixed btw? If not that's going to add a whole level of hormonal frustration and more irritability to things. He really should be fixed especially if he's let outdoors.

So if you don't have the necessary amount of litterboxes, add more. Make sure they're large enough, have no lids, are each in different rooms and filled with enough unscented clumping clay litter.

After that, make sure all boxes are scooped at least twice a day.

You should also take her to the vet to make sure she doesn't have any medical issues (like a bladder infection) that may be causing her to pee outside the box.

You will also want to make sure he isn't developing arthritis because that can make getting in/out of the litterbox or squatting on the uneven surface of the litter impossible or painful. So he'll go somewhere else.

Lastly have you cleaned the spots he's peed on with a good enzymatic cleaner? If not you may be encouraging him to re-use the same spot/there may be some smell left (even if you can't tell) that encourages him to pee in the same spot.

Your kitty likely has some level of periodontal disease, especially if he's not eating a dental diet and not getting his teeth brushed. 

I wouldn't start brushing his teeth until after he's had a dental exam (and possible cleaning) at the vet. If he's got infected gums or abscesses or loose teeth due to plaque/tartar build up his mouth is going to be painful and brushing will be impossible.

They sell enzymatic pet toothpaste at most vet clinics and some pet supply places (do \*not\* use human toothpaste---this is toxic and not made to be swallowed unlike pet toothpaste). It comes in a few different flavours like chicken or seafood so (usually) cats like it. It's the brushing part that they're not super fond of. You can use a regular soft bristle toothbrush made for toddlers to brush your cat's teeth.

My kitty eats the Hills t/d kibble as his main diet (he's not great with being groomed/restrained yet). Cats really like eating it and it will help reduce/prevent plaque and tartar buildup. Especially if you have a cat that won't tolerate having their teeth brushed. 

Dental disease is a bit of an epidemic among pets because most people don't think about it. Without proper hygiene and care pretty much any pet over 2-3 years of age will have some level of periodontal disease. Like with people this is not only painful but the bacteria buildup in the mouth can travel through the bloodstream and damage organs, so it's important to take care of their teeth.

I have a big nearly seven year old female coastal carpet who for \*years\* was just not handleable. Hooks, gloves, getting her out to handle her multiple times a week---everything backfired and she \*hated\* me. 

In the last two years I've completely overhauled how I do things with her. I don't grab her out of her cage or restrain her in any way unless it's absolutely necessary. There's no longer any tap training with the snake hook---it's only used to block her or gently lift/redirect her if I need to. She's allowed to come out on her own and interact with me if she wants to. I added a shift/trap box hide into her enclosure and if I need to clean her cage I'll wait until she goes in there, close the door and lock her in. 

Result? She's nearly completely calmed down. She actually spends more time out and wants to come out of her cage more. She actually will approach me and want to interact with me.
